## Notebooks

A **notebook** (Jupyter, or Google Colab, which runs Jupyter notebooks in a browser) is a document of **cells**. A code cell is sent to a running interpreter, called the **kernel**, and its output, including tables and figures, is saved in the document under the cell. Markdown cells hold text. With uv, `uv run --with jupyter jupyter lab` starts JupyterLab from a project folder ([uv documentation](#references)).

Notebooks combine the REPL's immediacy with a record of what was run, which is why data analysis and teaching use them. The NLP and Generative Models courses on this site come with notebooks. They have one trap that scripts do not: the kernel keeps every name from every cell you ran, in the order you ran them, which need not be the order on the page. A cell that uses a name defined in a cell further down, or one that you since deleted, works now and fails for the next reader. The execution counter next to each cell, `[3]`, records the order. Before sharing a notebook, restart the kernel and run all cells from the top; if it still works, its saved outputs are what the code produces.

A **content-addressed build** gives every action a key, the hash of its command line and of the contents of all its inputs, and keeps a cache from keys to outputs. Before running an action, the tool computes the key; if the cache has it, the output is copied from the cache, and the action does not run. Bazel ([Bazel documentation, Remote caching](#references)), Buck2, Pants and Nix work this way. Nothing in the project changed, and its build now contains different code. This is why the result of a resolution is written down. A **lockfile** (`uv.lock`, `package-lock.json`, `Cargo.lock`, `go.sum`) records the exact version of every package, direct and indirect, its source, and a hash of each file; an install from the lockfile reproduces the same set, and a downloaded file whose hash differs is rejected. The [Python course](/notes/python/modules-and-packages#lockfiles-and-reproducible-experiments) shows `uv.lock` in detail. The two files have different jobs: the ranges say what the code supports, the lockfile says what one build used. The lockfile is committed and changes only on purpose, in its own commit, usually opened as a pull request by a bot such as Dependabot or Renovate when a new version appears, so that the upgrade goes through the same tests as any other change.
## Reproducible builds

A lockfile fixes the inputs. That does not yet make the output repeatable. A build is **reproducible** if, given the same source code, build environment and build instructions, any party can recreate bit-for-bit identical copies of the artifacts ([Reproducible Builds project, Definitions](#references)). Three things commonly break it.

The convention `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` ([Reproducible Builds, SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH specification](#references)) gives tools one timestamp to use instead of the clock, usually the time of the last commit, which belongs to the source. GCC, Clang, and many archivers and documentation tools honour it; the program linked from `c.o` prints `calc, built Oct 22 2026 12:00:00`, the commit's time, on every rebuild.

**Order and metadata.** An archive records the order in which files were added, their modification times, and the owner's account. A tool that adds files in the order the file system lists them, stamps them with their current times and writes the time into the gzip header gives a new archive every run. `package.py` packs the same `dist/` folder both ways; the reproducible mode sorts the names, sets every time to `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`, clears the owner and writes no timestamp into the gzip header:
$ python3.14 package.py reproducible; touch dist/bin/calc; python3.14 package.py reproducible
reproducible 8ed98cea04ac6e10 1587 bytes
reproducible 8ed98cea04ac6e10 1587 bytes

Two default runs a second apart already differ; the reproducible ones agree even after a file's time changed. The same problem hides in build files: GNU make 3.82 to 4.2 returned `$(wildcard src/*.c)` in directory order, which differs between file systems, and so linked objects in a different order on different machines; the Makefile in the [Example](#example) wraps it in `$(sort …)`. Iteration over hash tables, whose order may vary from run to run, is the same trap inside a program.

**Why it matters.** A reproducible build makes the artifact checkable. If anyone who builds the tagged source gets the same hash as the published binary, the binary contains nothing that is not in the source. Two attacks show what that check is for. In the SolarWinds compromise, disclosed in December 2020, attackers did not change the source repository: malware on the build server inserted a backdoor into the product as it was compiled, and the company's own signed updates carried it to its customers ([CISA, 2021](#references)). In the xz-utils backdoor, found in March 2024 (CVE-2024-3094), the malicious build script was present only in the release tarballs, not in the Git repository, so a build from Git and a build from the tarball would have differed ([Freund, 2024](#references)). An independent rebuild that compares hashes catches both kinds. The [last note of the course](/notes/devops/incidents-and-security#the-supply-chain-sboms-signatures-and-slsa) builds the rest of the defence: bills of materials, signatures, and signed provenance graded by the levels of SLSA.

`v1.4.0-2-g0ecda82` is two commits after the tag `v1.4.0`, at commit `0ecda82` (the `g` stands for Git). A build from a working tree with uncommitted changes is marked `-dirty`, a version that no commit can reproduce and that a release pipeline should refuse. SemVer reserves the suffix after `+` for build metadata (`1.4.0+0ecda82`), which does not affect version ordering.

- **Reproducibility is a spectrum.** Bit-for-bit identity needs every tool in the chain to cooperate, and some (code signing, profile-guided optimization, nondeterministic linkers) need extra work. Many projects aim first for builds that are functionally the same, and use bit-for-bit reproducibility where the supply-chain check matters most.

- A build is reproducible if the same source, environment and instructions give identical bytes. Time, order and environment break it; `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`, sorting and pinned toolchains fix it. Independent rebuilds catch tampered builders and tampered release tarballs.

The [previous note](/notes/mlops/features-and-skew) made the input of training well defined: features that mean in training what they mean in serving, joined without information from the future. Training itself is still a sequence of runs, dozens of them, started from notebooks and scripts with slightly different settings, and one of them produces the model that goes to production. Months later someone asks which data that model was trained on, or a bug fix needs the same model retrained with one change, and the answer has to exist. This note is about making runs reproducible, recording them so that they can be compared and rerun, and keeping the chosen models in a registry that links each one back to the run that made it and forward to the deployment that serves it.

The usual starting point is a directory: `model_final.pkl`, `model_final_v2.pkl`, `model_final_v2_fixed.pkl`, and a spreadsheet of accuracies typed in by hand. The notebook that produced the deployed file has been edited since. The training data was the result of a query on a day nobody wrote down, against tables that have changed. The library versions were whatever was installed on one laptop. When the model misbehaves, nobody can say whether it was trained on the data that is suspected of being bad; when a fix is made, nobody can retrain "the same model plus the fix", because the same model cannot be produced again. And the file itself, a pickle, runs arbitrary code when it is loaded.
- **Code**: the commit hash, plus a flag or a diff when the working tree had uncommitted changes. A run from a dirty tree cannot be reproduced from the repository alone.

- **Data**: an immutable snapshot identifier or a content hash, as produced by the tools of the [data versioning note](/notes/mlops/data-quality-and-versioning#versioning-data-by-content). A table name is not a version; a query result on a moving table is not reproducible.

- **Environment**: the interpreter, the library versions pinned by a [lockfile](/notes/python/modules-and-packages#lockfiles-and-reproducible-experiments), and for full fidelity the digest of the [container image](/notes/devops/container-images#registries-tags-and-digests) the run executed in, which also fixes system libraries such as CUDA and BLAS.

- **Randomness**: the seeds of every generator, set before the model is built; the Deep Learning course lists the [sources of randomness and the pitfalls](/notes/deep-learning/training-in-practice#make-runs-reproducible).

Three levels of reproduction are worth distinguishing. A **bitwise** reproduction gives identical weights; it is achievable on one machine with a fixed environment and deterministic kernels, and the Example achieves it for a random forest. A **statistical** reproduction gives a model whose metrics fall within the spread over seeds; it is what survives a change of hardware or library version. A **conclusion** reproduction confirms that the claimed effect, "feature X helps", holds up with a fresh setup. The ACM's terminology for published research calls these repeatability (the same team and setup), reproducibility (another team, the same setup) and replicability (another team, another setup) ([ACM, 2020](#references)).

The tracker makes comparison a query instead of an archaeology: `mlflow.search_runs(filter_string="params.trees = '50' and metrics.accuracy > 0.94")` returns a table of runs, and the user interface plots metrics of selected runs side by side. Weights & Biases, Neptune, ClearML and Aim offer the same model with hosted services; DVC records experiments as Git commits beside the data versions. What none of them does is decide what to record: a run that reads an unversioned table is tracked perfectly and still cannot be reproduced. The practice that makes tracking useful, changing one thing at a time and writing down why a run was made, is the one the Deep Learning course describes under [tracking experiments](/notes/deep-learning/training-in-practice#track-every-experiment).

Key idea. A model is reproducible only if every input of its run has an identifier that the run records: commit, data snapshot, configuration, environment, seeds; and even then, results are identical only on the same hardware and software, and equivalent elsewhere only within the spread over seeds. A tracker records runs; a registry gives the few models that matter immutable numbered versions linked to their runs, and mutable aliases that deployments follow, so that promotion and rollback are pointer moves. Ship weights in formats that cannot execute code.

- **Bitwise reproducibility is narrow.** It holds on one hardware and software stack with deterministic kernels, often at a cost in speed; across GPUs, library versions or numbers of devices, only statistical reproduction is realistic.
- A model is a function of code, data, configuration, environment, randomness and hardware; record an identifier for each, or the run cannot be reproduced.
- Bitwise reproduction holds on a fixed stack; elsewhere, reproduce statistically, and judge differences against the spread over seeds and the standard error $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ of the test metric.

The arrangement that most teams start with looks like the wall of the [DevOps course](/notes/devops/what-devops-is#baseline-throw-it-over-the-wall), with a model in place of a release. # Sloth [![CI](https://github.com/slok/sloth/actions/workflows/ci.yaml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/slok/sloth/actions/workflows/ci.yaml) [![Go Report Card](https://goreportcard.com/badge/github.com/slok/sloth)](https://goreportcard.com/report/github.com/slok/sloth) [![Apache 2 licensed](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Apache2-blue.svg)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/slok/sloth/master/LICENSE) [![GitHub release (latest SemVer)](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/slok/sloth)](https://github.com/slok/sloth/releases/latest) ![Kubernetes release](https://img.shields.io/badge/Kubernetes-v1.35-green?logo=Kubernetes&style=flat&color=326CE5&logoColor=white) [![OpenSLO](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenSLO-v1alpha-green?color=4974EA&style=flat)](https://github.com/OpenSLO/OpenSLO#slo) ## Project status Sloth is actively maintained and in continuous development. We’re currently working on internal improvements to make Sloth even more extensible and adaptable to real-world use cases. While Sloth already supports custom SLI plugins, upcoming changes will bring more flexibility to how SLOs are generated, making it easier to adapt Sloth to your custom needs. Stay tuned for updates! ## Introduction Meet the easiest way to generate [SLOs][google-slo] for Prometheus. Sloth generates understandable, uniform and reliable Prometheus SLOs for any kind of service. Using a simple SLO spec that results in multiple metrics and [multi window multi burn][mwmb] alerts. https://sloth.dev ## Features - Simple, maintainable and understandable SLO spec. - Reliable SLO metrics and alerts. - Based on [Google SLO][google-slo] implementation and [multi window multi burn][mwmb] alerts framework. - Autogenerates Prometheus SLI recording rules in different time windows. - Autogenerates Prometheus SLO metadata rules. - Autogenerates Prometheus SLO [multi window multi burn][mwmb] alert rules (Page and warning). - SLO spec validation (including `validate` command for Gitops and CI). - Customization of labels, disabling different type of alerts... - A single way (uniform) of creating SLOs across all different services and teams. - Automatic [Grafana dashboard][grafana-dashboard] to see all your SLOs state. - Single binary and easy to use CLI. - Kubernetes ([Prometheus-operator]) support. - Kubernetes Controller/operator mode with CRDs. - Support different [SLI types](#sli-types-manifests). - Support for [SLI plugins](#sli-plugins) - A library with [common SLI plugins][common-sli-plugins]. - [OpenSLO] support. - Safe SLO period windows for 30 and 28 days by default. - Customizable SLO period windows for advanced use cases. ![Small Sloth SLO dashboard](docs/img/sloth_small_dashboard.png) ## Getting started Release the Sloth! ```bash sloth generate -i ./examples/getting-started.yml ``` ```yaml version: "prometheus/v1" service: "myservice" labels: owner: "myteam" repo: "myorg/myservice" tier: "2" slos: # We allow failing (5xx and 429) 1 request every 1000 requests (99.9%). - name: "requests-availability" objective: 99.9 description: "Common SLO based on availability for HTTP request responses." labels: category: availability sli: events: error_query: sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="myservice",code=~"(5..|429)"}[{{.window}}])) total_query: sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="myservice"}[{{.window}}])) alerting: name: "MyServiceHighErrorRate" labels: category: "availability" annotations: # Overwrite default Sloth SLO alert summmary on ticket and page alerts. summary: "High error rate on 'myservice' requests responses" page_alert: labels: severity: "pageteam" routing_key: "myteam" ticket_alert: labels: severity: "slack" slack_channel: "#alerts-myteam" ``` [This](examples/_gen/getting-started.yml) would be the result you would obtain from the above [spec example](examples/getting-started.yml). ## Documentation [Check the docs to know more about the usage, examples, and other handy features!][docs] ## SLI plugins Looking for common SLI plugins? Check [this repository][common-sli-plugins], if you are looking for the sli plugins docs, check [this][docs-sli-plugins] instead. ## Development and Contributing Check [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).
